title: The assistant's own Browser — built, tested, ready for your look

steps.path: The right side of a chat, once the assistant uses the browser
steps.headline: A Browser panel shows what the assistant's hidden browser is doing, live.
steps.changed: When the assistant browses, a panel opens beside the chat with a live picture of the page, its address, and Show window.
steps.notice: Nothing pops up on your screen: the browser works out of sight unless you press Show window. A globe button in the top bar reopens the panel.
steps.risk: The panel takes the same right-hand space as Session Files and Games, so opening one closes the others.

steps.path: Under the latest message, the first time the assistant clicks or types on a site
steps.headline: Before clicking or typing on a new site, the assistant asks you once for that chat.
steps.changed: A card asks to let the assistant use that site: Allow for this chat, Always allow the site, or Not now.
steps.notice: The same card appears in Claude Code chats and in chats with other models — one set of rules for both.
steps.risk: Browsing several new sites means one card per site; reading pages never asks.

steps.path: Under the latest message, when the next click looks like buying, sending or deleting
steps.headline: Anything that looks like buying, sending, posting or deleting asks every time.
steps.changed: A final-step card names the exact button and site, and only offers Allow this once or Don't allow.
steps.notice: This asks even on a site you chose Always allow for, and even when the chat is set not to ask about anything.
steps.risk: It judges from button words and how forms submit, so an oddly named button can slip by; the assistant is also told to confirm such steps with you in chat.

steps.path: Under the latest message, when the assistant needs you to sign in or solve a captcha
steps.headline: When a site needs you — a sign-in or a captcha — the assistant asks and waits.
steps.changed: A card shows the assistant's request with Show window (sign in in a real window), Show the browser, I can't do this and I'm done.
steps.notice: Sign-ins you make in the assistant's browser are remembered next time; it never uses your own browser's sign-ins unless you turn on My Chrome.
steps.risk: Showing the window restarts the browser; pages reopen, but anything typed and not yet sent is lost.

steps.headline: Settings → Browser: which browser, show a window, allowed sites and saved sign-ins.
steps.changed: A new Settings row opens the Browser's choices: the assistant's own browser or My Chrome, a Show a browser window switch, the sites you've always allowed, and Clear saved sign-ins.
steps.notice: It finds the Chrome, Edge, Chromium or Brave you already have; with none, it offers a one-time download of about 150 MB.
steps.risk: My Chrome is marked Experimental: it works with your real sign-ins and was tested only against a separately started Chrome, not your own.

steps.path: A new chat in the dev window
steps.headline: Ask the assistant to look something up on a real website — does it browse, ask you, and answer?
steps.changed: The window runs this branch end to end: a real model, a real browser on your computer, and the Browser's cards and panel.
steps.notice: Try both kinds of chat if you can: a Claude Code chat and a chat with another model. Both should show the same cards and panel.
steps.risk: It is a second window on your desktop; the browser it opens is separate from your own and from your installed YouCoded.

steps.path: What happens the first time the assistant browses
steps.headline: Should the browser work hidden by default, with the panel to watch it?
steps.today: The assistant browses out of sight; a panel beside the chat shows the page live, and Show window opens a real window.
steps.problem: A real window on top of your work is distracting, but some people want to watch every click.
steps.proposal: Keep hidden as the default and let anyone switch on Show a browser window in Settings.

options.label: Hidden by default
pros: Never takes your screen; you can still watch in the panel.
cons: A first-time user may not notice the panel unless it opens.

options.label: A window by default
pros: Obvious what the assistant is doing.
cons: Covers what you were working on every time it browses.

steps.path: Settings, then Browser, then My Chrome
steps.headline: Should My Chrome ship now as Experimental, or stay hidden until tested on your own Chrome?
steps.today: My Chrome lets the assistant open tabs in your running Chrome with your sign-ins, after you switch it on in Chrome and click Allow.
steps.problem: It is the riskiest option — the assistant can act as you on any site you're signed into — and it has only been tested against a separate Chrome, not yours.
steps.proposal: Ship it marked Experimental and off by default; it asks before every new site and never offers Always allow.

options.label: Ship as Experimental
pros: You get your real sign-ins when you want them.
cons: Untested on your own Chrome's switch until you try it.

options.label: Hide it for now
pros: No way to act as you by accident.
cons: Every site needs signing in again inside the assistant's browser.

steps.path: Any chat set to never ask (full auto / skip permissions)
steps.headline: Should the Browser's cards still ask in chats set to never ask?
steps.today: In a chat set to never ask, other tools run freely, but the Browser still asks per site and before final steps.
steps.problem: That breaks the never-ask promise, but a never-ask chat browsing with your sign-ins could buy or delete without you.
steps.proposal: Keep the final-step card in every mode; you choose whether the once-per-site card also stays.

options.label: Keep both cards
pros: Same safety everywhere; one rule to learn.
cons: Never-ask chats still pause once per new site.

options.label: Only final steps ask
cons: A never-ask chat can type into any site without asking.
